steps: For % yield: calculate theoretical yield (moles of limiting reactant → mole ratio → mass of product using Mr)
For atom economy: identify desired product and all products in the balanced equation
Apply: % atom economy = (Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all products) × 100
For limiting reactant: convert both reactant masses to moles; compare actual mole ratio to equation ratio
method_card.title: Yield and Atom Economy
method_card.content:
Two distinct calculations — easy to confuse, so know which question is being asked before you start.

Percentage yield compares what you actually got from a reaction to the maximum you could theoretically have made:

\[\% \text{ yield} = \dfrac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100\]

Theoretical yield is calculated from the limiting reactant using mole ratios and Mr values. Yield is always ≤ 100%.

Atom economy measures how much of the total mass of all reactants ends up in the desired product:

\[\% \text{ atom economy} = \dfrac{M_r \text{ of desired product}}{M_r \text{ of all products}} \times 100\]

Note: this uses Mr values from the balanced equation — you do not need actual masses. A reaction with only one product has 100% atom economy. By-products reduce atom economy.

Limiting reactant: the reactant that runs out first determines how much product can form. Find it by comparing the mole ratio from the equation to the moles actually present — the one that is present in smaller proportion relative to its coefficient is the limiting reactant.

Why do industries care? High atom economy means less waste and lower costs. Low yield means inefficiency — reactions may be reversible, product may be lost during purification, or a side reaction may occur.

exam_context.marks: 3–5 per calculation; may be combined with an evaluation of industrial trade-offs
exam_context.frequency: High — yield and atom economy appear most years at Higher Tier; atom economy sometimes at Foundation

gold.display: Consider the industrial production of iron: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for Fe. (Ar: Fe = 56, O = 16, C = 12)

misconceptions.message: 2 Fe = 2×56 = 112. 3 CO₂ = 3×44 = 132. Total products = 112 + 132 = 244. Atom economy = (112÷244)×100 = 45.9%. (Double-check you are using 2 moles of Fe and 3 moles of CO₂.)
Sum the Mr of ALL products using their coefficients: 2Fe (112) + 3CO₂ (132) = 244. Atom economy for Fe = (112÷244)×100 = 45.9%.

gold.display: 24.3 g of aluminium reacts with excess chlorine: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. The student collects 80.1 g of AlCl₃. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: Al = 27, Cl = 35.5)

misconceptions.message: Al:AlCl₃ ratio from equation is 2:2 = 1:1. One mole of Al gives one mole of AlCl₃.

gold.display: A pharmaceutical reaction produces the desired drug (Mr = 250) as well as a by-product (Mr = 150). The equation shows they form in a 1:1 ratio. Calculate the atom economy for the drug.

misconceptions.message: Total Mr of products = 250 + 150 = 400. Atom economy = (250÷400)×100 = 62.5%.

gold.display: Which reactant is the limiting reactant when 6.0 g of Mg reacts with 8.0 g of O₂? The equation is: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)
options: Mg, because it has the smaller mass
O₂, because it has the smaller mass
Mg, because the moles available are less than required by the mole ratio
O₂, because there is excess after the reaction

misconceptions.message: n(Mg) = 6÷24 = 0.25 mol. n(O₂) = 8÷32 = 0.25 mol. Ratio needed: 2 Mg : 1 O₂. With 0.25 mol O₂ you need 0.50 mol Mg but only have 0.25 mol — Mg is limiting.
Compare actual moles to the equation ratio. 0.25 mol Mg needs 0.125 mol O₂ — there is excess O₂, so Mg is the limiting reactant.

gold.display: A student reacts 6.5 g of zinc with excess hydrochloric acid: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. She collects 0.14 g of hydrogen gas. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: Zn = 65, H = 1)

misconceptions.message: n(Zn) = 6.5÷65 = 0.10 mol. Ratio 1:1 (Zn:H₂). Theoretical n(H₂) = 0.10 mol. Mr H₂ = 2. Theoretical mass = 0.10×2 = 0.20 g. % yield = (0.14÷0.20)×100 = 70%.
The question asks for yield of H₂, not ZnCl₂. Mr H₂ = 2. Theoretical = 0.10×2 = 0.20 g. % yield = (0.14÷0.20)×100 = 70%.

bronze.display: A student obtains 3.2 g of copper from a reaction. The theoretical yield is 4.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

misconceptions.message: % yield = (3.2 ÷ 4.0) × 100 = 80%. Do not divide theoretical by actual.

bronze.display: A reaction produces 5.6 g of iron oxide. The theoretical yield is 8.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
Consider: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. Which is the desired product if the aim is to make quicklime (CaO)?
options: CO₂
CaCO₃
CaO
Ca

misconceptions.message: CaO is quicklime — the product we want to collect.

bronze.display: In the reaction 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, the only product is water. What is the atom economy?
bronze.equation_hint: If there is only one product, all atoms end up in it.

misconceptions.message: When there is only one product, the atom economy is always 100% — every atom becomes part of the desired product.

bronze.display: A student expects to make 12.0 g of a product but only obtains 9.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
The theoretical yield of NaCl from a reaction is 5.85 g. The actual yield is 4.68 g. Calculate the percentage yield.
In the reaction: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, all reactant atoms end up in NH₃. What is the atom economy?
bronze.equation_hint: Only one product — all atoms go into it.

misconceptions.message: Only one product (NH₃) means atom economy = 100%.

bronze.display: Give one reason why the percentage yield of a reaction is less than 100%.
options: The Mr of the product is too large
Some product is lost during filtration or evaporation
Atom economy is always less than 100%
The reaction is endothermic

misconceptions.message: Yield is reduced by practical losses (spills, incomplete transfer, purification steps) or if the reaction is reversible or slow.

silver.display: Consider: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Calculate the atom economy for CO₂ as the desired product. (Ar: C = 12, O = 16, H = 1)
silver.equation_hint: % atom economy = Mr(desired product) ÷ sum of Mr of ALL products × 100. For 1 CO₂ + 2 H₂O.

misconceptions.message: Mr CO₂ = 44. 2×Mr H₂O = 2×18 = 36. Total = 80. Atom economy for CO₂ = (44÷80)×100 = 55%.
Sum ALL product Mr values with their coefficients: CO₂ (44) + 2×H₂O (36) = 80. Atom economy = (44÷80)×100 = 55%.

silver.display: Ethanol can be made by fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂. Calculate the atom economy for ethanol (C₂H₅OH). (Ar: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
silver.equation_hint: Total Mr of products = 2×Mr(C₂H₅OH) + 2×Mr(CO₂). Atom economy = 2×Mr(C₂H₅OH) ÷ total × 100.

misconceptions.message: Multiply each Mr by its coefficient in the balanced equation before summing.

silver.display: 12.0 g of magnesium reacts with excess oxygen: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. The student collects 18.0 g of MgO. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)
silver.equation_hint: Find theoretical yield: n(Mg) → mole ratio → n(MgO) → mass of MgO. Then % yield.

misconceptions.message: Find theoretical yield first using moles, then calculate % yield.

silver.display: Which of the following would increase the atom economy of an industrial process?
options: Filtering the product more carefully
Using a more concentrated reactant
Finding a reaction pathway that produces fewer by-products
Cooling the reaction mixture slowly

misconceptions.message: Atom economy depends on the balanced equation — the ratio of desired product Mr to total products Mr. Fewer by-products means more atoms end up where you want them.

silver.display: 5.0 g of Na is reacted with excess water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. 8.2 g of NaOH is produced. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: Na = 23, O = 16, H = 1)
In the Haber process, N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, the atom economy is 100%. Yet the yield is only around 15% per pass. Explain the difference between atom economy and percentage yield in one sentence.
options: Atom economy measures what fraction of reactant atoms end up in the desired product; yield measures how much product was actually obtained compared with the maximum possible
Atom economy and yield are the same thing measured differently
Yield measures wasted atoms; atom economy measures how fast the reaction goes
Atom economy is only relevant in industry; yield applies to school experiments

misconceptions.message: Atom economy is about the reaction equation (types of products). Yield is about what you actually collect compared with the theoretical maximum.

worked_examples.question: A reaction produces 4.5 g of product. The theoretical yield is 6.0 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

steps.label: Step 1 — Find Mr of the desired product
steps.content: Mr of MgO = 24 + 16 = 40. From the equation, 2 moles of MgO are produced, so total = 2 × 40 = 80.

steps.label: Step 2 — Find total Mr of all products
steps.content: The only product is MgO (2 moles), so total = 80.

steps.label: Answer
steps.content: Atom economy = 100% — only one product, so no waste.

worked_examples.question: Consider the reaction: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Calculate the atom economy for MgO. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16)

steps.label: Step 1 — Find moles of Mg (limiting reactant)
Step 2 — Use mole ratio to find theoretical moles of MgCl₂

worked_examples.question: 2.4 g of magnesium is reacted with excess dilute hydrochloric acid: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. The student collects 8.1 g of MgCl₂. Calculate (a) the theoretical yield and (b) the percentage yield. (Ar: Mg = 24, Cl = 35.5, H = 1)
